turns.doctor_question: Hello. I'm Dr. Smith. What brings you in to see me today?
turns.patient_response:
Hi, Dr. Smith. Well, honestly, my boss is the one who suggested—or, I guess, strongly recommended—that I come in. I've been doing general maintenance and repair for years, you know, fixing HVAC units, patching drywall, dealing with plumbing issues in these big commercial buildings. I know my way around a toolbox better than anyone on the crew, I really do, and I've always worked hard. But... well, the problem is I keep forgetting things. Important things. 

Like scheduled callbacks, for example. A tenant will call about a leaky pipe, I'll go in and fix the immediate issue, tell them I'll call back Tuesday with the timeline for the permanent replacement part, and then... it just completely leaves my brain. Gone. Or work orders. I'll get a stack of work orders in the morning, and I swear I look at them, but then I'll just completely miss one, or I'll do the repair and forget to actually log that I finished it. 

And it's not even just the big technical stuff, it's the basic follow-ups I promised people, too. Like telling the front desk I need access to a specific electrical room, or telling my supervisor I need to order more sealant. I mean, I have notes everywhere, inside my truck, on my clipboard, but it doesn't even matter because now it’s all just piled up so much. The backlog, the paperwork, the missed calls... it's a total mess. 

My supervisor actually sat me down last week because there's a lead technician spot opening up. It's a real chance for me to move up, finally get a little more authority and better pay, which I really need. But he basically said my work is suffering too much and work sent me here to get this figured out before I lose my shot at moving up entirely. He told me I'm a great mechanic but a terrible manager of my own schedule right now. So... yeah, that's why I'm here. I just can't seem to keep it all straight anymore, no matter how hard I try to remember.

symptom_reasoning.S001: The patient describes making careless mistakes at work, such as completely missing a work order from a stack or failing to log a completed repair.
symptom_reasoning.S005: The patient describes their work as a 'total mess' with a backlog of paperwork and missed calls, and notes their supervisor called them a 'terrible manager of my own schedule', indicating difficulty organizing tasks.
symptom_reasoning.S009: The patient explicitly states they keep forgetting important daily work activities, such as scheduled callbacks, logging finished work, and basic follow-ups they promised to people.

turns.doctor_question: Looking back at your school years or childhood, did you struggle with these same issues of forgetfulness, organization, or losing track of tasks back then, or is this a relatively new problem for you?
turns.patient_response:
Oh, no, it is definitely not new. Not at all. I mean, if I really sit back and think about it... I remember being exactly this way way back in grade school. I am talking long, long before I ever picked up a wrench or had to worry about work orders or job pressure or any of that adult stuff. It was just... always there. 

I remember my mom used to get so frustrated with me, and the teachers, well, they were always pulling my parents aside at parent-teacher conferences. They would always start with the exact same speech, you know, telling my folks that I was a bright girl and had so much potential, but then the other shoe would drop. It was always about how I just could not keep track of my things. I was constantly misplacing my papers. I would do the homework, or at least I think I did, and then I would just lose it between the kitchen table and my desk at school. It was like a black hole in my backpack. 

And directions? Forget it. The teacher would stand at the front of the room and give us three things to do, and I would maybe catch the first one, and then completely miss the rest of the directions. I would just be sitting there looking around trying to figure out what everyone else was doing. They constantly had to come over and tap my desk and give me reminders just to finish my classwork. I would be staring out the window or just... I don't know, my brain would be somewhere else entirely, and they would have to tell me to focus and get back to my worksheet. 

So, yeah, it has been a lifelong thing, it really has. I guess maybe it just didn't matter as much when the worst thing that happened was a bad grade on a spelling test, you know? You can kind of skate by when you're a kid. But now... now it is my livelihood on the line, and the stakes are just so much higher with this lead technician spot.

symptom_reasoning.S004: The patient describes missing parts of directions and needing reminders to finish classwork.
symptom_reasoning.S007: The patient reports constantly misplacing papers and losing homework between home and school.
symptom_reasoning.S008: The patient mentions staring out the window and their brain being somewhere else entirely during class.

turns.doctor_question: Looking back at your childhood, were you also physically restless, like having a hard time staying seated or feeling like you were driven by a motor?
turns.patient_response:
No, not really. I mean, I know some kids are like that, bouncing off the walls, tearing through the house, driving their parents crazy because they can't sit still for two seconds. My brother was actually a little bit like that, always needing to be outside, always running around, constantly getting into scrapes because he just couldn't slow down. But me? No, I wasn't like that at all. 

I was actually pretty quiet, physically speaking. I could sit in my chair for hours, honestly. The problem was never my body wanting to get up and run away, it was my brain. Like, my body would be sitting perfectly still at my desk, but my mind would be a million miles away, thinking about the clouds outside, or a show I watched the night before, or just... nothing. Just completely zoned out. 

I remember my dad used to say I was "in my own little world." He'd be talking to me at the dinner table, and I'd be sitting right there, not fidgeting, not squirming, just staring at my peas, and he'd have to wave his hand in front of my face to get my attention. So, no, I never had that feeling of being driven by a motor or needing to jump out of my skin. It was always just the daydreaming, the drifting off, the losing track of time while I was sitting perfectly still. Even now, if I'm sitting in the truck waiting for a parts delivery, I don't feel like I need to pace around the parking lot. I just end up staring at the steering wheel and completely forgetting to check the invoice list I was supposed to be reviewing. So, yeah, the physical restlessness, the bouncing around... that was never really my issue. It's always been the mental drift.

symptom_reasoning.S003: The patient describes not seeming to listen when spoken to directly, noting his dad had to wave a hand in front of his face to get his attention at the dinner table.
symptom_reasoning.S008: The patient describes his mind drifting off, daydreaming, and being distracted by unrelated thoughts like the clouds or a TV show.
symptom_reasoning.S009: The patient mentions forgetting to check an invoice list he was supposed to be reviewing at work.
symptom_reasoning.S010: The patient explicitly denies fidgeting or squirming while seated.
symptom_reasoning.S011: The patient denies having the urge to leave his seat, stating he could sit in his chair for hours.
symptom_reasoning.S012: The patient explicitly denies experiencing physical restlessness.
symptom_reasoning.S014: The patient explicitly denies ever having the feeling of being driven by a motor.
